results.corrected_claim: "Get to know the new design system" is WWDC25 session 356. Session 284 is "Build a UIKit app with the new design". The sentence "However, glass can not sample other glass, so having nearby glass elements in different containers will result in inconsistent behavior." is from session 323, "Build a SwiftUI app with the new design". The Sources list in 02-hig-principles.md (L171-175) does not cite 323. createwithswift.com is a third-party (secondary) source.
results.notes: Verified from the Liquid Glass technology overview DocC JSON, which lists wwdc2025-219 Meet Liquid Glass, wwdc2025-356 Get to know the new design system, wwdc2025-323 Build a SwiftUI app with the new design, wwdc2025-284 Build a UIKit app with the new design, and wwdc2025-310 (AppKit). Each title was also confirmed on its WWDC video page. The 323 transcript has the 'can not sample' sentence verbatim; the 284 and 356 transcripts do not. Corrections to the finding: (1) the same mislabel is also at 01-api-reference.md L585, and 01 L3 cites 'sessions 219, 284, 323'; (2) 'which the skill does not cite' is true only for 02's Sources list, because 01-api-reference.md L586 does cite 323. Related: in 323 that sentence is about nearby glass in different containers behaving inconsistently, not about stacked glass turning into 'flat blur' (02 L66). Session 219 gives a different reason: 'always avoid glass on glass. Stacking Liquid Glass elements on top of each other can quickly make the interface feel cluttered and confusing.'

results.corrected_claim: No Apple primary source publishes the skill's radii (20-28, 12-16), padding (12/12, 16/10, 20/14, 28/18, 20/20), GlassEffectContainer spacing tiers (8-12, 16-20, 24-32, 40+) or font roles. Nothing supports 'the values their first-party apps converge on'. What Apple does publish: WWDC25 356 'fixed shapes have a constant corner radius.' / 'Capsules use a radius that's half the height of the container.' / 'concentric shapes calculate their radius by subtracting padding from the parent's.' HIG Accessibility: 'about 12 points of padding around elements that include a bezel. For elements without a bezel, about 24 points of padding works well around the element's visible edges.' This is spacing between controls to reduce mis-taps, not padding inside a glass element. HIG Buttons: 'a hit region of at least 44x44 pt'. HIG Materials: 'consider adding a dark dimming layer of 35% opacity' under clear glass over bright content.
results.notes: Both of the finding's quotes are verbatim. The 356 transcript contains no numeric radius, padding or spacing values. HIG Buttons, Layout, Materials and Typography (DocC JSON) give no corner-radius or glass padding/spacing tokens. The GlassEffectContainer doc only says 'The higher the spacing, the sooner blending begins as the shapes approach each other.' Apple's own samples contradict the skill's spacing tiers: the morphing example in 'Applying Liquid Glass to custom views' uses GlassEffectContainer(spacing: 40.0) for elements that do morph, while the skill files 40+ under 'distinct, non-morphing siblings'. The glassEffectTransition sample uses spacing 10.0. A universal negative cannot be proven, but every primary page checked lacks these tokens.

results.corrected_claim: No Apple source says iOS 26 system fonts were retuned for legibility over glass. WWDC25 356: 'Typography has been refined to strengthen clarity and structure, now bolder and left-aligned to improve readability in key moments like alerts and onboarding.' HIG Typography change log, December 16, 2025: 'Added emphasized weights to the Dynamic Type style specifications for each platform.' For legibility on glass, Apple describes adaptive color, not new fonts. WWDC25 219: 'To maintain legibility, symbols and glyphs on top of Liquid Glass, do the same. They flip from light to dark and vice versa, mirroring the glass's behavior to maximize contrast.'
results.notes: The 356 quote is verbatim, from a paragraph that also says system colors were adjusted 'so that they work in harmony with Liquid Glass'. That is about colors, not fonts. The finding's HIG quote drops the trailing 'for each platform' (minor). HIG Typography and HIG Materials have no sentence about fonts being retuned for glass. HIG What's New lists no typography changes in June or September 2026 (iOS 27). Session 219 adds that this light/dark flip applies 'from labels, text and fully tinted buttons... to the time on your lock screen'. A corrected skill line could cite that adaptive behavior and the emphasized Dynamic Type weights.

results.corrected_claim: Apple's glass morph sample uses plain `withAnimation { isExpanded.toggle() }`. The default animation is `spring(response:dampingFraction:blendDuration:)` with response 0.55, dampingFraction 1.0 and blendDuration 0.0, which is critically damped and does not bounce. The Applying article says: 'The glassEffectID(_:in:) and glassEffectTransition(_:) modifiers only affect their content during view hierarchy transitions or animations.' No Apple source makes .bouncy the glass default or forbids .linear. For Reduce Motion, HIG Accessibility lists 'Tightening animation springs to reduce bounce effects', and WWDC25 219 says 'Reduced Motion decreases the intensity of some effects and disables any elastic properties for the material.'
results.notes: The 'only affect their content...' sentence is in the Applying article, not on the glassEffectID or glassEffectTransition symbol pages. Those pages say SwiftUI uses the identifier 'to animate shapes to and from each other during transitions'. The words 'bouncy', 'spring' and 'linear' do not appear in the Applying article, the Landmarks sample page, the glassEffectID/glassEffectTransition pages, the WWDC25 323 code samples (which contain no animation call at all), or HIG Motion. GitHub mirrors of Apple's Landmarks BadgesView.swift (secondary) show `withAnimation { isExpanded.toggle() }`, and one copy shows `withAnimation(reduceMotion ? nil : .default)`. The skill's line numbers are accurate: 03 L102, L105, L111; 04 L94; 07 #13 (L308-319); checklist L45-46. Elasticity is built into the material itself (219: 'Liquid Glass responds to interaction by instantly flexing and energizing with light'); it does not come from the developer's animation curve.

results.corrected_claim: Verified: iPhone Duo is a new device class (HIG, September 9, 2026: 'iPhone Duo is the first folding iPhone'), and the checklist's Devices section (L68-73) does not mention it. HIG quote in full: 'On iPhone Duo, toolbars, tab bars, and navigation controls that are typically at the top and bottom of the display move to the side, preserving vertical space for content and keeping controls within easy reach. The exception is the inner display in portrait, which has enough vertical space to keep standard horizontal bars.' The ReservedRegion and Device Hub quotes are verbatim. SwiftUI's September 2026 notes add `var toolbarVerticalEdge: HorizontalEdge? { get }`, `nonisolated func toolbarVerticalBehavior(_ behavior: ToolbarVerticalBehavior) -> some View` and `struct ReservedRegion`. All three list iOS and iPadOS introducedAt 27.1 with beta: true, so they need iOS 27.1 and do not exist in iOS 27.0. Not verified: the finding says 03-design-tokens L132-141 assumes top nav bar and bottom tab bar, but that Z-stack section never mentions top or bottom. The bottom-edge assumptions are actually in patterns/glass-floating-toolbar.md L61 (.safeAreaInset(edge: .bottom)), patterns/glass-card-stack.md L62 (FAB in .overlay(alignment: .bottomTrailing)) and 04-motion L238-240.
results.notes: Read from the HIG DocC JSON; the page change log reads 'September 9, 2026 New page'. HIG What's New, September 18, 2026: 'New product bezels for iPhone Duo and all the new iPhone 18 models.' The custom-floating-glass point is supported. HIG: 'For custom components, ReservedRegion (SwiftUI) and ReservedRegion (UIKit) provide a way to reposition content away from reserved regions.' and 'Use safe areas to make sure controls don't cover your content, including controls on the opposite edge.' toolbarVerticalEdge's abstract says 'Use it to position custom bars or other UI relative to the system's bar placement', with a FloatingToolPalette example, and it returns nil where no vertical bar is ever used. The toolbarVerticalBehavior doc says the vertical bar's leading or trailing safe-area inset is added or removed, so overlays that respect the safe area move clear of the side bar automatically. Also new in September 2026: axisBehavior(_:), toolbarVerticalCompressionBehavior(_:), ArrangementView and onHingeChange(isEnabled:_:). iPhone 11 on iOS 27 is backed only by secondary sources (AppleInsider, 9to5Mac, Tom's Guide, June 8, 2026); apple.com could not be reached for a primary confirmation.

results.corrected_claim: Glass, Glass.clear, Glass.identity, View.glassEffect(_:in:) and GlassEffectContainer list only iOS, iPadOS, Mac Catalyst, macOS, tvOS and watchOS, each introduced at 26.0 and not beta. visionOS is absent. glassEffectID, glassEffectTransition, GlassButtonStyle and GlassProminentButtonStyle lack visionOS too. visionOS has its own API, `glassBackgroundEffect(in:displayMode:)` (visionOS 1.0 only). The tvOS note in Adopting Liquid Glass is verbatim: 'Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) and newer models support Liquid Glass effects. On older devices, your app maintains its current appearance.' Remove visionOS 26+ from SKILL.md L5 and 'visionOS 26' from the L3 trigger list, or redirect visionOS work to glassBackgroundEffect.
results.notes: I checked the raw metadata.platforms JSON for Glass, Glass.clear and Glass.identity, and the platform lists for glassEffect(_:in:), GlassEffectContainer, glassEffectID, glassEffectTransition and both glass button styles. Declarations match: `nonisolated func glassEffect(_ glass: Glass = .regular, in shape: some Shape = DefaultGlassEffectShape()) -> some View` and `@MainActor @preconcurrency struct GlassEffectContainer<Content> where Content : View`. The Adopting article itself names only 'iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, and watchOS'. Current (iOS 27-era) docs still add no visionOS entry for these symbols, and SwiftUI's June 2026 notes contain no Liquid Glass or visionOS glass changes.
